title: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Effect of temperature”. Scope: physiological processes, especially growth, in plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-22: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Competing mechanistic models can be formulated and tested in systems with repeated thermal exposure and stress measurements. Existing public datasets are fragmented and usually resolve only selected organisms or proxy damage variables, limiting causal discrimination.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use time-resolved growth and damage or survival markers across temperatures to fit a model combining low-temperature kinetic acceleration with cumulative high-temperature injury, and compare it against a primary optimum-response model. Superior out-of-sample fit and temporal accumulation of damage would support the proposed resultant mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Growth and cumulative damage are rarely measured together.

The proposed mechanism spans diverse processes and taxa.

Acclimation, enzyme kinetics and resource limitation produce similar optimum curves.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.75
data existence: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Acute versus chronic thermal performance can in principle separate cumulative damage from an instantaneous optimum, and growth-versus-temperature data exist to support pieces of that contrast. Public compilations store a rate or a single temperature coefficient, not the time course of damage, and several molecular rivals fit the same optimum curve. The mechanistic claim is only partly operational and only partly supplied with data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Separate a short-term accelerating effect of temperature from a cumulative damaging effect, for example by comparing brief exposures above a putative optimum with long exposures. The claim predicts that an optimum curve appears only when both effects act. An instantaneous equilibrium optimum, with no extra damage from duration, would count against that two-process account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Protein denaturation and other single mechanisms also produce an optimum curve.

Cumulative damage or fatigue is not a column beside growth rate.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
